Prescription flu medications causing halucinations and psychosis or acne medications causing depression, sexual disfunction, and possibly even being fatal...Is that normal for all medications for the same kind of ailments and your doctor know not to prescribe it outside of certain cases or is it marketing trying to make cash off of a sub-standard product?

Sort of. Most medications do have some terrifying potential side effects - it's just that those side effects are either one in several million (in other words, "struck by lighting" type frequency), only happen in people with some other condition (e.g. fluoroquinolone antibiotics and diabetes), result from drug interactions (e.g. aspirin and ibuprofen, acetazolamide and all sorts of other stuff), or have another non-drug trigger (e.g SSRIs and grapefruit juice). The "worst" case for any drug is almost always death, but only in the midst of a perfect storm of other factors that everyone involved completely ignored.

So long as your prescribing physician and pharmacist are responsible and the patient isn't an idiot, most of the worst side effects on the list are completely irrelevant to any specific case. However, when speaking to a wider audience (rather than a specific patient) it's impossible to know which bits do and don't potentially apply, so you can't just go skipping them even if they're rare. On one hand, doing so would be medically irresponsible, but on the other hand (particularly in the U.S.) you'll almost certainly get sued by the one idiot who didn't read the pamphlet, didn't listen to his doctor and did see your ad.

All true, of course. In a perfect world, this is a good system. In practical application, it can be dangerous. But then, there's another side that tends to get overlooked.

It should come as no surprise that the patent laws in this country are completely nuts. As is government regulation. Not that either should be done away with, but both get heavy handed and rarely consider forces outside of their little domain. As such, drug companies get screwed. Developing a drug takes years and a lot of FDA oversight and approval- which, all in all, is a good thing. Except. In order to maintain a patent, a drug company must patent a formula immediately. They don't know if it works, if it works with hideous side effects, or if it's the next cure-all for mankind. From then, the clock is ticking. 7 years. Actually, I think 10 under one of the only good things the ACA did. Time from discovery to market is 3-5 years, which makes for a very limited amount of time to turn a profit before the generics come out. The generics are an important part of the process- I can only afford the only migraine drug that I've found to work because it recently went generic. But if the drug company doesn't turn a profit in that time, they start losing money and no one gets anything new. It's actually kind of funny that Viagra and Cialis fund research into medicine that's actually useful.

Point of all this is that, sure, we gets ads for drugs that smooth over the little annoyances of life. And some for the moderate-sized problems in life. But all this plays a second role. They keep drug companies solvent in order to produce medicine that may not look great in a commercial, can actually save lives.

I'm not saying I have any answers. Increasing the time a drug can stay under patent helps, but that's obviously not a solution that we can keep going back to. If we allow Disney-style patents on drugs (Disney works very hard to make sure that Mickey will never go out of trademark), then we never get the more-affordable generics. But if we don't allow for enough time to make a profit, we don't get anymore drugs. TV/Magazine ads help with this.
